title: C, G, e le doppie
summary: Hard vs soft c/g (ci/chi, gi/ghi), the gn/gli/sc sounds, and why double consonants change the word

blocks.title: C and G: it's the next letter that decides
blocks.body: *c* and *g* are **hard** (like *k* and *g* in 'go') before *a, o, u* — and **soft** (like *ch* in 'church' and *g* in 'gem') before *e* and *i*. So *cane* = KA-ne but *cena* = CHE-na. To keep a hard sound before *e/i*, Italian slips in an **h**: *che, chi, ghe, ghi*.

blocks.explain: *c* before *e* or *i* goes soft: *cena* = CHE-na. Before *a/o/u* it would be hard.

blocks.title: Three sounds English doesn't have
blocks.body: **gn** = the *ny* in 'canyon': *gnocchi*, *signora*. **gli** = a wet *lli*, like the *lli* in 'million' but softer: *famiglia*, *figlio*. **sc** before *e/i* = *sh*: *scienza*, *pesce*. Before *a/o/u* though, *sc* is just *sk*: *scala*.

blocks.title: Double consonants are real
blocks.body: A **double consonant** is genuinely held longer, and it changes the word. *pala* (shovel) vs *palla* (ball). *nono* (ninth) vs *nonno* (grandfather). Lean on the doubled sound — a beat longer — or you'll say the wrong word.
blocks.callout: *Ho un anno* = 'I have a year (of age)'. *Ho un ano* means something very different. Hold the double.

pairs.note: Hold the ll a fraction longer for palla.
The doubled nn is a real, longer sound.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type the word for 'ice cream'.

blocks.hint: That wet *gli* sound in the middle.
blocks.explain: *famiglia* — the *gli* is a soft, wet *lli*, not a hard g-l.
*nonno* (double n) = grandfather. *nono* (single n) = ninth. The doubled sound matters.

blocks.prompt: Which sound was hardest — gn, gli, sc, or holding a double consonant? Type two words you'll practise out loud today.
